message:
I run deliveries for a small furniture restorer and I've got a few things to sort for tomorrow.

Can you suggest a name for our new delivery van (staff vote, nothing rude)?

Tomorrow the van can't leave the depot before 08:30 and must be back by 12:00. Three drops, each takes 15 minutes to unload. Drop A has a delivery window of 09:00 to 10:00. Drop B is a shop that needs its delivery done before it opens at 09:30. Drop C is an office that won't accept anything before 11:00. Driving times: depot to A 30 min, depot to B 20 min, depot to C 45 min, A to B 25 min, A to C 40 min, B to C 50 min. The driver also needs a 30-minute break somewhere before 12:00. What order should he go in, and what's the timeline?

Could you also rewrite our delivery text so it sounds friendlier than "Driver arriving. Be in."? List three things the driver should check on furniture before handing it over. Should we give customers a paper delivery note or an emailed one? And define "proof of delivery" in a line for our new part-timer. One more thing: we're thinking of texting customers the evening before with a rough arrival time. Could you draft that evening-before text too, keeping it under 160 characters so it goes as a single message?
response:
## Van name ideas
- **Dovetail**
- **The Chesterfield**
- **Sideboard Express**
- **Vanity Unit** (a cheeky but clean pun)
- **Grandfather Clock**: it always turns up on time, in theory

## Tomorrow's route: B → A → C

This is the only order that works. B has to come first, because going to A first means reaching B at 09:40, after the shop opens. C has to come last, because it won't accept anything before 11:00.

| Time | Activity |
|---|---|
| 08:30 | Leave depot |
| 08:50 | Arrive at **B**, unload (done by 09:05, before the 09:30 opening ✅) |
| 09:05 | Drive to A (25 min) |
| 09:30 | Arrive at **A**, unload (done by 09:45, inside the 09:00–10:00 window ✅) |
| 09:45 | Drive to C (40 min) |
| 10:25 | Arrive near **C**. **30-minute break** (10:25–10:55), then wait |
| 11:00 | Unload at **C** (done by 11:15 ✅) |
| 11:15 | Drive back to depot (45 min, assuming the return takes as long as the trip out) |
| **12:00** | **Back at depot, with no time to spare** |

**This route has zero slack.** C can't start before 11:00 and the drive back takes 45 minutes. Even a perfect run gets back at exactly 12:00, so a slow handover or a bit of traffic on the way back means he's late. Ways to build in some margin:
- **Ask C whether they'd accept at 10:30.** The driver is outside from 10:25 anyway. That would get him back around 11:30.
- **Check whether the 12:00 return is firm**, or whether 12:15 would be acceptable.
- **Call C beforehand** so someone is ready to receive the delivery at 11:00 sharp.

## Friendlier "on the way" text
> Hi [Name], it's [Driver] from [Company]. I'm on my way with your furniture and should be with you in about [X] minutes. See you soon!

## Three checks before handover
1. **Condition.** Look for scratches, dents and marks on the finish, and compare against the photos taken before it left the workshop.
2. **Completeness.** Make sure every part is there and fitted: shelves, legs, handles, keys, glass and fixings.
3. **Function and stability.** Check that it stands level without wobbling, and that drawers and doors open and close smoothly.

Ideally, do these checks *with* the customer before they sign.

## Paper or email delivery note?
Email is better, ideally with a signature on the driver's phone and a photo of the item in place. It's quicker, harder to lose, and gives you a timestamped record. Keep a few paper notes in the van for customers without email.

## Proof of delivery (for the part-timer)
"A signed and dated record, ideally with a photo, showing the item reached the right person at the right address in good condition."

## Evening-before text
> Hi Sam, Oakhill Restoration here. Your delivery is due tomorrow, roughly 9-10am. We'll text when the driver sets off. Questions? Call 01234 567890

This comes to **146 characters** with the example name, company and number. Two tips to keep it to a single message:
- **Check the length with your real details.** Long customer or company names add up.
- **Use plain characters only.** Use a straight apostrophe (') and a plain hyphen (-). Avoid emoji, curly quotes and long dashes, which can cut the limit to 70 characters.
